newsitem.title: USA: Broader Liggett tobacco pact expected soon.
newsitem.headline: Broader Liggett tobacco pact expected soon.

text.p: By Gail Appleson, Law Correspondent

Talks aimed at a broader settlement of smoking lawsuits between Liggett Group Inc. and nearly two dozen states have intensified and a deal could be reached soon, sources familiar with negotiations said Wednesday.

The talks, which involve Liggett's proposal to turn over highly sensitive industry documents, have picked up ahead of the first anniversary of Liggett's break with the industry to become the first cigarette maker to settle smoking litigation.

On March 13, 1996, Liggett, the smallest of the nation's major tobacco companies, agreed to settle a federal class-action lawsuit in New Orleans and two days later reached an accord with five states that had sued the industry to recoup the costs of providing health care for poor smokers.

But 22 state attorneys general and the lieutenant governor of Alabama have now sued the industry to recoup Medicaid costs for treating smokers and Liggett wants a broader pact that would satisfy a larger number of states.
"Talks with Liggett have been ongoing," said Mike Moore, Mississippi's attorney general who is a leader in the negotiations.
Still, a settlement between more states and Liggett, owned by Bennett LeBow's Brooke Group Inc., would not necessarily point to an industrywide settlement that would include other tobacco companies.

Last year Liggett broke ranks by settling with Mississippi, Florida, Massachusetts, West Virginia and Louisiana. It paid them a total of $1 million immediately and agreed to pay a total of $4 million to be split by the states over the next nine years.
It also agreed to pay the five settling states 2.5 percent of its annual pretax income over the next 25 years.
Moore said Liggett's second payment to Mississippi was due by Saturday. Neither he nor a LeBow spokesman would discuss the talks further.

Sources close to the negotiations involving Liggett said the parties were close to an agreement. They said they had hoped to reach a deal before the anniversary of last year's settlement but now an accord was not expected until after the end of next week.
"The documents are key," said one source. "I understand they could be quite damaging."

LeBow would want as many states as possible to agree to drop their suits against Liggett before he would turn over the papers. Some states, in particular Minnesota, previously have raised doubts about a proposed settlement.

While the sources expressed optimism a settlement could be reached between Liggett and most of the states, they said the larger tobacco companies have made no effort to settle with the states or lawyers representing others suing the industry.
They said that if an industrywide settlement could be reached it would not be for quite a long time.

Rumours over a possible industrywide settlement began to swirl last month when the Wall Street brokerage house Sanford C. Bernstein issued a report saying the industry was likely to agree to pay into a settlement fund in exchange for protection against smoking-related lawsuits.

When cigarette companies recently hired two politically connected Washington law firms and a powerful public relations firm to handle tobacco litigation matters, that further fed speculation about a settlement.

The National Journal, a Washington-based publication covering policy issues, reported the firms had been hired specifically to develop plans for a comprehensive settlement of the industry's legal and regulatory problems.

Just last week, when B.A.T Industries Plc released its 1996 earnings, it reiterated a previous statement that it was prepared to evaluate "any sensible proposal" for an industrywide settlement that would end U.S. litigation.
But one source close to the attorneys general said he thought cigarette makers were just trying to bolster their stock prices by dropping hints a settlement was near.
"If investors think a settlement is happening soon they are spinning in the wind. This is all pie in the sky so far," he said.
Mississippi's Moore said that while he felt the tobacco industry was serious about a settlement, he expected to take his state's Medicaid case to trial in June.
"Time is running out for them," he said. "My case is 80 days away."
